https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce85.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The Sudanese army recently rallied its supporters as it continues to fight the Rapid Support Forces By Damian Zane Published 3 hours ago Thirty-five people were killed in a drone strike by the Sudanese army on a traditional court session in the north of the Darfur region, a local rights organisation has said. Dozens more were reported injured in Sunday afternoon's attack. The Emergency Lawyers Group, which monitors violence against civilians, said the attack occurred in Ghara al-Zawiya village that is controlled by the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The army has not commented. The RSF holds most of Darfur, in the west of the country, as the two sides continue to fight in the three-year-long civil war that has devastated the country, killed tens of thousands of people and forced millions from their homes. Sunday's "court session was being held under a tree with the participation of local community leaders," a witness is quoted by the AFP news agency as saying. Four tribal leaders and two RSF commanders were among those killed in the attack, according to the witness. The privately owned Darfur 24 website quoted a local resident who said that two drones flew over the town "before launching more than four missiles". The Emergency Lawyers Group called for an investigation into the drone strike and condemned the targeting of the court saying that attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure are a "grave violation of international humanitarian law". It also noted that drones are being increasingly used "to target civilian areas and gatherings, which exacerbates the risks faced by the population". The RSF has also been accused of war crimes including drone attacks on civilians over the past three years. The paramilitary group's siege and attack on el-Fasher, one of Darfur's main cities, last year bore the "hallmarks of genocide" according to a UN fact-finding mission. The RSF has denied the accusations. https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: BERLIN — Europe's reserves of natural gas are running dangerously low, risking fresh energy woes if the Iran war rages on and cold spells drive up heating demand over winter. But the continent's top energy user doesn't seem too bothered. Germany is the EU's biggest vulnerability because its sheer size means gas shortfalls there could be felt in neighboring countries, driving up prices across the bloc if it fails to restore its reserves. Advertisement Advertisement That's prompted growing calls for Berlin to do the unthinkable: intervene outright to direct its state-controlled energy giants to buy gas at any price, abandoning years of free-market doctrine on energy policy. So far, the government has refused to budge, even as it falls short of EU targets and faces the risk of physical supply shortages as early as November. It's a gamble that the markets will figure everything out, even as war and hot weather distort traditional incentives and upend global supply chains. "Storage levels are not only exceptionally low for this time of year, but historically low," said Sebastian Heinermann, the managing director of Germany’s top gas storage association, INES. But Germany, he warned, is still relying on an outdated, market-oriented approach to refill its reserves, even when there are "hardly any market-economic incentives left." Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, EU countries have been required to hit gas storage targets of 90 percent of national capacity by winter to prevent serious supply shortfalls. The EU lowered that target to 80 percent following the outbreak of the Iran war to prevent panic buying . Typically, refilling is the responsibility of traders and utilities, which buy gas cheap in the summer to store and then sell in the winter for a profit. But buyers say higher summer prices as a result of the Iran war and climate change have upended that dynamic, leaving gas reserves across the bloc at around 58 percent of national capacity, 16 percentage points below the five-year historical average and the lowest level since 2011. Advertisement Advertisement The low reserves have already added to the increased pressure on gas prices linked to renewed tensions around the Strait of Hormuz, with the European natural gas benchmark now consistently higher than it was for the first four months of the Iran war. The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, has said the bloc faces no winter supply risks. But a report by energy analytics firm Rapidan projects that reserves will rise to only 65 percent of total storage capacity by November, arguing that hitting the EU's target by winter won't be possible without "materially higher prices." That risk has been exacerbated, analysts say, by the bloc’s move in recent years to replace its long-term supply deals with Russia with short-term purchases of globally traded liquefied natural gas. These seaborne cargoes are highly mobile and go to the highest bidder — leaving buyers more exposed to volatility on international markets, especially in the wake of the loss of key supplies from Qatar and rising demand in Asia . A tanker passes through the Strait of Hormuz on Feb. 25, 2026. | Fadel Senna/AFP via Getty Images Germany, the bloc's largest gas consumer, has seen its reserves fill up even more slowly than others, in part thanks to its more hands-off, market-led approach to restocking than many of its neighbors. As a result, reserves stood at only 47 percent of national capacity in August, according to the latest data — the lowest fill level since records began. That's especially worrying as the country's reserves are important for the bloc as a whole, representing over 20 percent of the EU's storage capacity. Nevertheless, Berlin is staying the course. While its energy ministry has acknowledged the country's historically low reserves, it has refused to intervene to direct its main state-controlled gas buyers, SEFE and Uniper, to buy gas at current prices to ensure its targets are met, instead of waiting for market conditions to improve. "It is the responsibility of companies and traders to fill the storage facilities for the winter," a spokesperson for the German energy ministry told POLITICO. "Government-led filling of the storage facilities would further constrain the gas market and drive prices even higher. The supply situation over the coming months would actually deteriorate." Advertisement Advertisement Whether this is the right approach will become clearer by winter, said Laurent Ruseckas, a senior gas analyst at S&P Global. If temperatures are unseasonably low, traders may be forced to buy additional supplies at late notice, driving up prices, especially if the Strait of Hormuz remains closed. On the other hand, intervening could raise prices prematurely if winter turns out to be mild. "If you start buying now to get storage to some politically predetermined level you’re making prices higher now to get insurance that you won’t get higher prices in the winter when it’s cold," said Ruseckas. Germany's reluctance to move quickly also highlights the difficulty the EU's fragmented energy sector has in competing with more centralized Asian economies that have acted more quickly to secure supplies, consistently outbidding European countries even as their reserves run low. Others warn that physical supply strains are also possible. Heinermann, of INES, warned that even filling the country’s reserves to 76 percent of capacity — which SEFE says is achievable — would not necessarily meet its supply needs if winter is "exceptionally cold." That could ripple out to neighboring countries to which Germany is treaty-bound to provide emergency gas assistance, including Austria, Switzerland, Italy and Denmark. Heinermann called on the German government to encourage faster restocking by lowering network charges at storage facilities or abolishing the conversion levy, fees imposed for the conversion of gas on national grids. Berlin has already unveiled plans for a new emergency gas stockpile, but that will only cover 10 percent of the country's gas capacity and kick off officially next summer. It's no surprise that other major gas consumers have already waded into the private sector. The Netherlands, another free-market champion suffering from low gas reserves, earlier this summer allocated €1.2 billion for its state energy company, EBN, to more swiftly top up its reserves. Advertisement Advertisement But Berlin's energy giants are sticking to their guns — for now. A spokesperson for SEFE told POLITICO that even though "international conflicts" could weigh on European storage levels, the 70 percent target "remains achievable" without intervention. He pointed out that 78 percent of German storage capacity has already been booked, though acknowledged that doesn't necessarily translate to actual volumes of gas stored. Regulatory measures could be useful if "necessary" but could distort markets and increase costs, he added, without specifying what. A Uniper spokesperson was less confident, warning it would be "increasingly challenging to reach the target storage levels before the winter season starts" at the current rate of filling. But she too stopped short of calling for intervention, arguing instead for better incentives for refilling — mirroring growing calls from gas lobbyists in Brussels to scrap the rules outright.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: The FBI has drawn concern about a perceived loosening of recruitment requirements as the it seeks to replenish its ranks. Photograph: Douliery Olivier/Abaca/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen The FBI has drawn concern about a perceived loosening of recruitment requirements as the it seeks to replenish its ranks. Photograph: Douliery Olivier/Abaca/Shutterstock FBI FBI no longer treating applicants’ experience with sex workers as automatic bar against hiring Bureau will still dismiss those engaged with sex workers within past 10 years, three or more times overall, or while in public safety capacity Associated Press Sat 29 Aug 2026 10.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The FBI is dropping a categorical hiring ban on applicants who have had sexual encounters with sex workers and will instead consider in a more holistic manner at least some candidates who have engaged in the practice in the past, according to people familiar with the matter. The move away from an automatic disqualification falls along a continuum of evolving recruitment standards within federal law enforcement and at the buttoned-up bureau, which several years ago relaxed its approach to candidates’ past marijuana use and has drawn more recent concern among some current and former agents about a perceived loosening of recruitment requirements as it seeks to replenish its ranks. The bureau still intends to dismiss applicants who are revealed during the vetting process to have engaged with sex workers within the last 10 years, three or more times overall, or while in a position of trust, such as in public safety capacity, according to guidance issued this past spring and described by a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to discuss internal decision-making and spoke on condition of anonymity. Man posed as 49ers player to scam women out of $1.3m, FBI says Read more For others, it will allow for consideration of the context of the conduct rather than treat it as grounds for an automatic rejection during the FBI’s hiring process. The practical impact is not immediately clear since many who have solicited or accepted sex work may still be either immediately disqualified or weeded out upon further scrutiny from FBI polygraphers and security officials. The FBI said the change was meant to account for the fact that some otherwise suitable candidates, including service members, may have engaged in the practice in places where it is legal – and to accommodate applicants who may done so when they were much younger or have themselves been victims of sexual abuse. “It is false to suggest criminal behavior like this is no longer disqualifying at the FBI. Any applicant who has engaged in criminal sexual acts like those referenced would of course not be eligible for employment, and it is ridiculous to suggest otherwise,” the FBI said in a statement that described the background check process as “wide-ranging and extensive”. “The FBI has and always will maintain some of the highest suitability standards for its applicants and employees in the US government,” the statement added. Even so, the shift is being made at a time when current and former officials worry that the FBI, and the federal justice department more generally, have eased recruitment requirements while facing a mass personnel exodus brought on by retirements, voluntary resignations and firings. The bureau, for instance, has taken steps to make it easier for its own professional staff to become agents and has offered a truncated training academy for applicants from other federal law enforcement agencies. “If they’re moving the bar for sexual encounters to include prostitution, what is that saying about the applicant pool? They’re trying to bring in more people, which to me indicates that the applicant pool is extremely shallow right now,” said Daniel Brunner, a retired FBI agent who spent two decades in the bureau. In 2015, then attorney general Eric Holder issued a memo reiterating that all justice department employees were prohibited from soliciting or accepting sex work, including in places where it was legal. But both before and since that directive, the FBI and other federal law enforcement agencies have confronted periodic episodes in which agents serving abroad have been accused of sexual encounters with sex workers. As recently as the summer of 2025, for instance, the justice department inspector general substantiated allegations that a supervisory special agent solicited and engaged sex workers on multiple occasions while overseas and used a bureau-issued cellphone for the transactions. Chris Piehota, a retired top FBI executive, said he would be more troubled if the bureau were to loosen its standards for current employees who require periodic renewals of their security clearances. But he said he could understand the FBI leaning “toward leniency” for actions taken as a teenager or college student. “I don’t think you get a better or worse candidate from something you did in your college years,” Piehota said. “That’s why they have the screening process, that’s why they have the vetting process. And the people who do the recruiting and hiring, they look at all those things.” Applicants to the FBI undergo a multistep application and vetting process that includes, among other things, a background check, a detailed questionnaire, credit checks, interviews with neighbors and colleagues, and a polygraph test. The comprehensive regimen is meant to uncover any prior criminal conduct in an applicant’s past as well as embarrassing personal information that could make an employee vulnerable to blackmail. Felony convictions, domestic violence convictions, failure of a urinalysis and violating bureau’s drug policies are among factors treated as automatic disqualifiers. Though the new guidance will allow for a broader and more contextual evaluation of applicants who disclose past experience with sex work during their polygraph admission, such an admission has historically been typically regarded as a “death knell” for potential employees at agencies including the FBI, the CIA and the NSA, said Daniel Meyer, a Washington lawyer with the Tully Rinckey law firm who specializes in the background check and the security clearance process. Witkoff and Kushner met Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin on Saturday. Putin called the situation “difficult” but said contacts with Washington were useful. Russia and Ukraine also agreed to refrain temporarily from strikes on each other’s capitals while the American delegation conducts its diplomatic mission. The limited truce is the clearest immediate result of the latest effort. It is not, however, a broader ceasefire, and the fundamental issues that have blocked previous negotiations remain unresolved. Russia continues to demand Ukrainian territorial concessions and the abandonment of Kyiv’s NATO ambitions. Ukraine has rejected those terms. The new mission therefore represents less a fresh peace process than the revival of a diplomatic effort that stalled earlier this year. February 2025: Trump opens direct diplomacy with Putin and Zelenskyy Trump began his second-term Ukraine diplomacy with direct telephone conversations with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. U.S. and Russian officials subsequently met in Riyadh on Feb. 18, 2025, marking the beginning of a new American effort to establish negotiations. The talks immediately generated controversy because Ukraine was not represented in the first U.S.-Russia meeting. Trump then pushed Moscow and Kyiv toward a broader ceasefire. After U.S.-Ukraine discussions in Saudi Arabia, Kyiv agreed to a proposed 30-day ceasefire. Russia did not accept the proposal in full. Instead, Moscow agreed to narrower measures involving attacks on energy infrastructure and later discussions concerning the Black Sea. The March negotiations were therefore a diplomatic achievement, but not a peace settlement. By April, frustration inside the Trump administration had become public. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was prepared to abandon the mediation effort unless there was rapid progress. Trump similarly warned that the United States could “take a pass” if either side made an agreement impossible. This was one of the clearest moments when Washington threatened to end its involvement. European governments were concerned that Trump might leave the negotiations before Russia had made meaningful concessions. Trump subsequently pushed Moscow and Kyiv toward direct negotiations. The most significant result was a series of Russia-Ukraine meetings in Istanbul in May and June. The talks produced a major prisoner exchange but failed to produce a ceasefire or political settlement. Trump announced in May that Russia and Ukraine would begin immediate negotiations following his call with Putin, but the two sides remained far apart. Trump then intensified his personal diplomacy with Putin. Witkoff made repeated trips to Moscow before Trump and Putin met in Alaska in August 2025. The Alaska summit was one of the most important moments of Trump’s peace effort, but it ended without a ceasefire agreement. European leaders nevertheless welcomed Trump’s willingness to engage Putin. In a joint statement, the leaders of France, Germany, Britain, Italy, Finland and Poland, together with senior EU officials, said they welcomed Trump’s efforts to stop the fighting and pursue a “just and lasting peace.” But Europe also established important limits. The leaders insisted that Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity had to be protected and that Ukraine could not be excluded from decisions concerning its future. They also rejected the idea that Russia should have a veto over Ukraine’s European or NATO aspirations. After Alaska, Trump attempted to move toward a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy, followed by a possible trilateral summit involving all three presidents. The initiative failed to produce the expected breakthrough. In October, Trump cancelled a planned meeting with Putin in Budapest, saying that the timing was wrong and that there had been insufficient diplomatic progress. He said the meeting “didn’t feel right” because the two sides were not getting to the point necessary for an agreement. Russia had rejected an immediate ceasefire, contributing to the collapse of momentum. The Trump administration then moved toward a more detailed written peace framework. A U.S. proposal initially containing 28 points generated substantial criticism in Ukraine, Europe and Washington because critics said it gave Russia too many concessions. Republican lawmakers, including Sen. Roger Wicker and Rep. Don Bacon, publicly criticized elements of the plan and questioned whether the proposal rewarded Russian aggression. The document was subsequently revised. JLL: Quantum Computing Is Already Creating a New Real Estate Market Nonproliferation Risks of the U.S.-Saudi Nuclear Cooperation Agreement By December, American, Ukrainian, Russian and European officials were working around a revised 20-point framework. Negotiators reported progress on security guarantees, economic reconstruction and other issues, although territory remained unresolved. The diplomatic process continued into 2026. In January, Witkoff and Kushner met Putin and discussed further U.S.-Russia-Ukraine negotiations. Territorial disputes remained the central obstacle. In early February, Russia and Ukraine held another round of U.S.-brokered negotiations in Abu Dhabi. The talks were described by Ukrainian officials as productive, but there was no comprehensive settlement. On Feb. 17-18, the negotiating process moved to Geneva, where Witkoff and Kushner again represented the Trump administration. The talks were part of an increasingly complicated diplomatic effort involving multiple international crises. Those were the last U.S.-mediated Russia-Ukraine peace talks before the latest September initiative . After months in which the diplomatic process largely stalled, Trump has now restarted the effort. Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Moscow on Saturday and met Putin. They are scheduled to travel to Kyiv for talks with Zelenskyy. Trump said the envoys were carrying a “concrete proposal” to end the war, although the administration has not publicly disclosed its full contents. Has Trump actually succeeded at anything? Yes — but not at ending the war. Trump’s diplomatic efforts have produced several limited agreements and humanitarian results , including prisoner exchanges and temporary arrangements concerning energy infrastructure. The most important tangible achievement has been keeping direct negotiations alive between Russia and Ukraine. The talks have also produced major prisoner exchanges. The negotiations in 2025 and 2026 demonstrated that Moscow and Kyiv can reach narrow agreements even when they cannot resolve the central political dispute. But Trump has not achieved a general ceasefire or a peace agreement . The March 2025 energy and Black Sea arrangements were partial measures, not an end to the war. The Istanbul negotiations produced prisoner exchanges, not peace. The Alaska summit produced no ceasefire. The later U.S.-brokered negotiations also failed to resolve the territorial question. And the September 2026 initiative has only produced a temporary agreement to limit attacks on Moscow and Kyiv during the envoys’ visits. How many times has Trump said the negotiations were over? The answer requires an important correction. Trump has not repeatedly made a formal declaration that “the negotiations are over.” The previous characterization of a specific number of occasions was too broad. What Trump and his administration have repeatedly done is threaten to walk away from the negotiations or impose a deadline for progress. The clearest example came in April 2025, when Trump and Rubio said the United States could abandon the peace effort unless progress came within days. Trump again increased the pressure in July 2025, giving Russia a much shorter deadline to make progress toward ending the war. On July 28, he cut an earlier 50-day deadline to roughly 10 or 12 days and threatened additional sanctions. Yet Trump did not permanently leave the process. Indeed, on July 15, when the BBC asked whether he was finished dealing with Putin, Trump explicitly answered that he was “not done with him.” He said he was disappointed with Putin but intended to continue working on the problem. Trump also said he believed a deal had appeared possible with Russia four separate times , underscoring how often his expectations of an imminent breakthrough had failed to materialize. In October, Trump cancelled the planned Budapest summit with Putin because he believed another meeting would not produce progress. But even then he said the two could meet in the future. Europe’s reaction: Support for Trump, but skepticism about the deal European leaders have generally supported Trump’s attempt to engage Putin, while remaining deeply concerned about the terms of any settlement. European leaders welcomed Trump’s effort but insisted that Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity could not be sacrificed for a quick agreement. They also backed continued European pressure on Russia. Later, European governments became more openly concerned about proposals they believed were too favorable to Moscow. In December 2025, European leaders rallied behind Zelenskyy after U.S.-Ukrainian discussions over an earlier peace proposal that had been criticized as overly favorable to Russia. Europe’s fundamental position has therefore been consistent: Trump’s diplomacy is welcome, but peace cannot simply mean accepting Russia’s territorial demands. What do Trump’s U.S. critics say? Trump’s critics have focused on three main concerns. The first is that the administration may be offering Russia too much in exchange for too little . That criticism was particularly strong after the 28-point proposal emerged in late 2025. Republican lawmakers themselves objected to elements they believed could reward Russian aggression. The second criticism concerns American leverage . Some analysts argue that repeatedly threatening to walk away from negotiations can weaken Washington’s position if Putin believes the United States is more eager for an agreement than Russia is. The third is the composition of Trump’s negotiating team. Witkoff and Kushner have become central figures in the process, despite not being traditional career diplomats. Reuters reported that experts and officials questioned whether the administration was trying to manage extraordinarily complicated negotiations with a relatively small diplomatic apparatus. At the same time, Trump’s approach has supporters who argue that conventional diplomacy had failed and that direct engagement with Putin is necessary precisely because the Russian president has shown little willingness to respond to traditional diplomatic pressure. What are the chances this time? The latest mission contains one potentially important difference : both Russia and Ukraine have agreed to temporarily stop strikes against the other’s capital during the American delegation’s diplomatic activity. Putin personally received Witkoff and Kushner, and the Russian president publicly described continued contacts with Washington as useful. That is a small but genuine diplomatic opening. Russia is under greater economic and domestic strain from the war than it was at the beginning of Trump’s current diplomatic campaign. Ukraine is demonstrating an increasing ability to strike deep inside Russian territory. Yet Moscow’s fundamental negotiating demands remain largely unchanged. The latest talks will show whether that balance is finally beginning to shift. Putin can no longer wage the war while assuming that Russia’s major cities, energy infrastructure and commercial centers will remain largely insulated from Ukrainian retaliation. That could eventually strengthen Trump’s negotiating leverage. It could also have the opposite effect if the Kremlin concludes that military escalation is necessary to force Ukraine to stop the attacks. For the latest peace initiative to succeed, Trump therefore needs more than another meeting with Putin. He needs to determine whether the growing costs of the war inside Russia have changed the Kremlin’s calculation — or whether Putin remains prepared to absorb those costs in pursuit of his territorial objectives. That is likely to be one of the most important questions facing Witkoff and Kushner as they move from Moscow to Kyiv. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y0.text: Figure caption, Watch: CCTV shows Turkey school shooting suspect with weapon By Orla Guerin Â and Â Michael Sheils McNamee Published 22 September 2026, 10:00 BST Updated 11:42 BST Eleven people have been injured in a shooting outside a high school in Turkey, with police detaining a 15-year-old male suspect. Two people were left in critical conditions after a gunman opened fire before fleeing on Tuesday morning, It happened at the Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in the western province of Manisa, with the injured reportedly all students. The suspect's mother, father, and grandfather - who reportedly owned the weapon - have also been detained, according to the country's justice minister AkÄ±n GÃ¼rlek. It is the third school shooting in Turkey this year and comes as the government continues to grapple with how to address the recent spate of violence. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The incident saw a response from a number of different state agencies CCTV footage appeared to show the suspect walking through empty streets checking a shotgun, which is clearly visible. He is casually dressed and appears unhurried. Later footage showed the apparent suspect, who is reportedly a student at the school, running from the scene with the weapon still in hand. The motive behind the attack was not immediately clear. According to Turkish law, the teenager is required to appear before a court before being officially arrested. In a statement, Turkey's education ministry said the incident had "deeply saddened our nation, and our educational community in particular". It said that three national investigators from the ministry had been sent to Manisa. Two deadly school shootings in April caused outrage in Turkey and led to new security measures for the 2026-2027 academic year, including tighter gun controls. Before then, the country did not have a history of school shootings. In an attack in Kahramanmaras, a 14-year-old killed nine students aged 10 and 11, and one teacher. The gunman died at the scene. https://www.jpost.com/archaeology/articl.text: A prehistoric sanctuary discovered near Chelby in the Czech Republic is one of Central Europe's oldest monuments, according to research shared earlier this summer from the University of West Bohemia (UWB).The site has been dated to be over 6,500 years old, making it 1,000 years older than Stonehenge.The circular enclosure measures to 230 meters in diameter, featuring an over 2.5 meters deep ditch and twelve irregularly spaced entrances. "Circular enclosures are completely unknown in our region for this period, which already makes the site exceptional,” explained Petr Krišt of UWB's Archaeology Department who is leading the research.“But when we began to analyze the positioning of the entrances in detail, it became clear that their arrangement was not random,” he said. “Their geometry creates a system that made it possible to observe the most significant moments of the solar and lunar cycles.”While similar to Stonehenge in function, Czech site is olderArchaeologists have found two main observation points at the Czech structure, connecting the sunrise at the summer solstice with sunset at the winter solstice in one, while the other is set in elation with the moon's extreme positions on the horizon during its approximately 18-year cycle.A similar arrangement can be seen at Stonehenge.However, according to the research team's latest findings, the Czech structure is significantly older than the famed British site.“For prehistoric farming communities, the connection between sunrise and the summer solstice symbolized a beginning, while sunset and the winter solstice represented an ending,” stated Krištuf. “The same principle can be seen along Stonehenge's main axis. We can now see that the sanctuary at Chleby was designed similarly, more than a thousand years earlier.”Krištuf explained that the millennium older date came from radiocarbon dating of materials found at Chelby.“We assume that they may originally have decorated monumental gateways leading into the enclosure,” added archaeologist Jan Turek, who is involved in the research on behalf of Charles University. “The cult of the bull was an important religious symbol among the first farming communities and is known from many parts of prehistoric Europe.”Remains of Bronze Age burials also found at sitePrevious excavations at the site uncovered the remains of approximately 18 people in the ditch, later identified as a Bronze Age Únětice culture burial. Current research, however, indicates that the site's role later changed. “While Stonehenge experienced repeated periods of renewed use and is still associated, for example, with Celtic druids, the first results from Chleby suggest the opposite development,” noted Krištuf. “By the Iron Age, the monument appears to have definitively lost its original significance. The ditch was gradually filled in, and an ordinary settlement was established on the site of the former sanctuary.”The research will from now focus on analyzing soil from the site to aid in the understanding of how it was used during different eras, explained Jan Fišer of the University of Hradec Králové, who is also participating in the research.“In addition to artifacts and the remains of the dead, people leave chemical traces in the soil. These can help us understand how this exceptional site was used during different periods of prehistory,” said Fišer.The research is part of the international Long-term Land Use Dynamics within the Areas of Prehistoric Ritual Places project. It is being carried out in cooperation with the University of West Bohemia in Pilsen, Charles University and the University of Hradec Králové.
